opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to be careful not to read too much into a flat curve. When people see a benchmark where performance barely moves as you scale, the tempting conclusion is that there's some fundamental wall, some capability that scale just can't reach. Sometimes that's true, but often it isn't.

One common pattern is that the benchmark measures something that only shows up once a bunch of component skills all reach some threshold. If a task requires, say, five steps chained together and you need every step right, then modest improvements in each step barely change your end-to-end score. Underneath, the model is getting steadily better, but the metric is all-or-nothing, so it looks flat and then suddenly jumps. A lot of the so-called emergent abilities look like this when you examine them with a more continuous metric, like the log-probability of the correct answer rather than exact-match accuracy.

A second issue is that the scale-up you're looking at might simply be too small. If you go from one model to another that's two or three times bigger, that's a tiny step on the log scale that matters for these trends. Many capabilities improve roughly linearly in the log of compute, so you might need one or two orders of magnitude before the change is visible against the noise. Benchmarks also have noise floors, especially small ones with a few hundred questions, so a real but modest improvement can get swamped.

Third, sometimes the benchmark is genuinely hard in a way that's out of distribution for the training data, or the prompting setup handicaps the model. Then the bottleneck isn't parameters or compute so much as the data or the elicitation. You see this when a change in prompting, tool use, or a bit of fine-tuning unlocks large gains the raw scale-up didn't show. So a flat curve can tell you more about how you're measuring than about what the model could do.

And finally, there are cases where it really does reflect a limitation of the current recipe, where you need a different kind of training signal, like reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks or longer reasoning at inference time, rather than just more pretraining. That's important to know, but historically these have tended to be addressed by changes that are themselves scalable, rather than being permanent walls.

So my general stance is to look at the full trend across many model sizes, prefer smoother metrics where you can, ask whether the scale-up was large enough to expect a visible change, and only then conclude there's a real plateau. The track record of people declaring that some benchmark proves scaling has hit its limits isn't very good. Quite a few of those benchmarks were saturated a few years later.

r001.rationale: It says a benchmark may be genuinely hard because it is out of distribution for the training data, making data a bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It mentions data as a possible bottleneck and says fine-tuning can unlock gains, but does not clearly state that adding relevant training data can do so.

r003.rationale: It says changes in tool use can unlock large gains when scaling alone did not show them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd want to do is resist the temptation to read too much into it. When you see a flat line on some hard benchmark as you scale up compute, there are really a few different stories that could be going on, and they have quite different implications.

One story is that the benchmark is measuring something that just isn't very sensitive to the dimensions along which you're scaling. A lot of these hard benchmarks are constructed to have a threshold-like structure, where you need to get many steps right in a row, and if your per-step accuracy is going up smoothly but is still below some critical level, the aggregate score barely moves. Then at some point you cross that threshold and the score jumps. So what looks like "no improvement" is often improvement that's hidden by the way the metric is constructed. If you look at log-probabilities on the correct answers, or partial credit, you frequently see a smooth trend underneath the flat headline number.

A second story is that the benchmark is contaminated or saturated in some odd way, or that it's testing something very narrow where the training distribution just doesn't have much relevant signal. Scaling gives you more of what's in the data, so if the capability isn't well represented, you shouldn't expect much from scale alone.

And the third story, which is the one people often jump to, is that there's some genuine limitation of the paradigm, that you've hit a wall. I'm quite skeptical of that interpretation in most individual cases, mainly because the track record of "scaling won't get you X" claims has been pretty poor. Almost every time someone has pointed to a specific benchmark and said this one won't yield to scale, it has, sometimes with a bit of a lag, sometimes with changes in how you elicit the capability, like chain-of-thought or better post-training.

So my overall take is that a single flat result on a hard benchmark is weak evidence about the fundamental trajectory. What I'd pay much more attention to is whether the flatness persists across many different benchmarks, across multiple orders of magnitude of compute, and after people have made a serious effort to elicit the capability. If you saw that pattern broadly, that would be something. But one hard benchmark not moving is, more often than not, telling you something about the benchmark rather than about the limits of scaling.

r001.rationale: It says the capability may not be well represented in the training distribution, leaving little relevant signal for scaling to use.

r002.rationale: It does not state that adding relevant training data can unlock progress.

r003.rationale: It does not mention access to basic tools as a way to unlock progress.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what you infer from that. A benchmark can show very little improvement even when the model’s underlying capabilities are improving, because the way you measure performance doesn’t necessarily capture that progress.

Suppose a task requires getting ten steps right, and you only give the model credit if it gets all ten right. You might substantially improve its ability to do each individual step while still seeing almost no successful completions. Then, as you scale further, you can suddenly start seeing successes. The measured performance looks like a breakthrough, even though the underlying improvement was gradual.

So I’d want to look at more than just the final score. Is the model getting closer to the correct answer? Is it succeeding on simpler versions of the task? Is the probability it assigns to the correct answer increasing? Those can help distinguish a genuine lack of progress from progress that the benchmark isn’t sensitive enough to reveal.

Of course, that doesn’t mean scaling will inevitably solve the task. A flat result is evidence worth taking seriously. But by itself, it’s not enough to establish that you’ve hit a fundamental limit.

r001.rationale: The response attributes flat benchmark results to measurement insensitivity, not inadequate representation of the task in training data.

r002.rationale: It does not say that adding relevant training data can unlock progress.

r003.rationale: It does not say that access to basic tools can unlock progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what you infer from that. A benchmark can show very little improvement even when the underlying capabilities are improving substantially, particularly if it only rewards getting a difficult problem completely right.

Imagine a task that requires twenty steps, and the model has to get every step right to succeed. Improving its reliability on each step might still leave its overall success rate very low. Eventually, those improvements can translate into a fairly sharp increase in benchmark performance. So a flat stretch doesn’t necessarily tell you that scaling has stopped working.

But it also isn’t evidence that a breakthrough is inevitable. You’d want to look at partial progress, performance on related tasks, and whether the model is actually improving at the components that matter. The important distinction is between a limitation of the model and a limitation of what the benchmark lets us observe.
